$comment: Performance budgets, measured in CI on every push. See scripts/perf-budget.mjs.
These are ceilings, not targets. A number here should be comfortably above
today's measurement and comfortably below the point at which a phone on a
hotel wifi starts to suffer — a budget set to the current value flags every
commit and gets raised reflexively until it means nothing.
Raising one is a deliberate act with a reason attached, in the same commit
as whatever needed the room. That is the entire mechanism: not that the
numbers are perfect, but that growing past them has to be noticed.

bundles.name: app JavaScript (gzipped)
bundles.why: The one number a phone on a bad connection actually feels. Today ~140KB. Raised from 140KB, deliberately and with the reason attached: the ceiling had 0.2KB of headroom, which is a budget that fails the next commit whatever that commit is, and a number nobody can land under stops being a budget and becomes a coin toss. 148KB keeps roughly a second of 3G as the bound while leaving room to work in. It is not permission to grow: the next lane that needs more should be shrinking this rather than raising it again, and the Draft screen — 2,700 lines, the largest thing in here — is where that work is.

bundles.name: app CSS (gzipped)
bundles.why: Render-blocking, so it is worse per byte than the JavaScript. Today ~7.7KB.

bundles.name: HTML shell
bundles.why: The document itself. Today ~1.6KB; growth here usually means something got inlined that should not have been.

bundles.name: everything the browser must fetch to render (gzipped)
bundles.why: The total, so splitting one large file into three does not quietly pass three budgets. Demo Mode is the one thing left out, because it is genuinely not on the render path — and it has a ceiling of its own directly below, so the exclusion buys nobody any headroom.

bundles.name: Demo Mode, fetched only when a scenario is opened (gzipped)
bundles.why: Scenario fixtures and the engines that read them. Nothing on a page load can reach these — every path to them is a dynamic import behind Settings or an explicit ?demo= — so they are budgeted apart from the shell rather than against it. Today ~117KB, up from ~69KB when the Matchup screen landed: the five matchup scenarios pull in the distribution model, the correlation factors and the simulator, which is the cost of rehearsing that screen through the production engine rather than reimplementing it. Raised from 108KB by the DST lane, deliberately and here rather than reflexively later: the defence scoring table and the defence projection add ~2.2KB to this chunk because Demo Mode runs the real start/sit engine, and at 108KB that left 0.4KB of headroom — a ceiling the next unrelated commit would have failed against, which is how a budget stops meaning anything. Raised again from 115KB by the waiver claim planner integration, for the same reason and with the same reluctance: the demo waivers handler calls the same `buildWaiverClaimPlan` the live one does, which pulls the whole of `core/waivers/planner` — the roster-utility simulation, the add-specific drop cost, the pair search, the spine-and-fallback structure and the outcome tree — into this chunk for ~9KB. The alternative was a Demo Mode whose Waivers screen is missing its headline card, which is a worse demo than an ideal one is a better bundle; and reimplementing the plan for the demo would be exactly the second model this repository refuses to keep honest. The app-JavaScript chunk paid ~0.7KB for the same feature, because the wording is written on the server and only the component and its types reach the browser. 124KB restores roughly the proportional headroom the app-JavaScript budget carries. Note that the DST *fixture* is not in this number: `demo/fixtures/dst.ts` is reachable only from tests, so the bundler leaves it out. It has a ceiling all the same: fixtures are the easiest thing in this repository to add carelessly, and the day this fails is the day they should start being loaded per scenario rather than per family. Raised again from 124KB by the demo refresh, and for the third time the reason is that the demo runs a production engine rather than a copy of one: the defence planner and its outlook (~7KB), the manager-intelligence readers the ledger is fed to — transaction profiles, trade tendencies, draft tendencies and the bid summariser (~8KB) — and the slate and ledger fixtures themselves (~3KB). The render path paid nothing for any of it, and that was not free either: `weekRange` moved out of `core/dst/planner.ts` into `core/dst/weeks.ts` in the same change, because it was the one runtime import the render path took from the planner, and the moment Demo Mode ran `planDst` for real the bundler placed the whole defence model — and the start/sit engine behind it — in the entry chunk. 25KB of model on every page load, to print `Weeks 15–17`. The split is what keeps the app-JavaScript number identical to what it was before this lane. Raised again from 150KB by the trade ladder, and for the fourth time the reason is the same one: the demo answers `/api/leagues/:id/trades/ladder` through `buildLadderFor` and `buildLadder` — the four lineup passes and the rungs over them — rather than through a hand-written mirror of them, which brings `core/trades/ladder.ts`, `ladderInputs.ts` and the consolidation read into this chunk for ~1.8KB. The alternative was a Demo Mode whose new negotiation fold answers with an error, which is not a demo of anything; and a second ladder written for the demo is exactly the second model this repository refuses to keep honest. The render path paid ~1.2KB for the same feature — the fold, the rung formatter and the sample gate — against 9.4KB of headroom, and no engine crossed into it, because every number the card draws arrives on the wire already computed. 156KB restores roughly the proportional headroom the app-JavaScript budget carries; at 150KB this chunk had 1.0KB left, which is a ceiling the next unrelated commit would have failed against.

$flowComment: Interaction budgets, enforced by e2e/performance.spec.ts against a real
WebKit iPhone viewport. Wall-clock in CI is noisy — a shared runner can be
three times slower than a laptop — so these are deliberately generous and
exist to catch a flow going from milliseconds to seconds, not to police
